analysis.one_liner: Bans oil companies from withholding fuel to raise prices, and lets US courts sue OPEC.
analysis.headline: The bill never left the House Judiciary Committee — no markup, no vote, before Congress ended in January 2007.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have made it illegal for oil companies to hold back or divert fuel supplies with the aim of driving up prices or creating shortages. It ordered antitrust agencies to study oil-industry mergers and whether past required divestitures actually worked, set up a federal-state task force to investigate oil industry information sharing, and stripped foreign oil cartels like OPEC of immunity from US antitrust lawsuits. It died in committee without ever getting a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Drivers and businesses that buy gasoline and heating fuel, who pay the price when oil companies or foreign cartels restrict supply to push prices up. State attorneys general would gain a partner task force for price-gouging investigations.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Drivers and anyone buying gasoline or heating fuel

how_it_helps.text: Makes it unlawful to refuse to sell, export, or divert existing petroleum or natural gas supplies with the primary intention of raising prices or creating a shortage.
Directs the Justice Department and FTC to study whether antitrust merger rules should be tightened for oil and gas companies, and report to Congress within 270 days.
Orders a GAO study of whether required divestitures in past oil and gas antitrust settlements actually restored competition, with agencies required to consider further action.
Creates a joint federal-state task force to investigate information sharing among oil and gas companies, which can feed price-fixing and collusion cases.

Enacts the NOPEC provision: makes it illegal for foreign states acting together, such as OPEC members, to limit oil production or set prices affecting the US market, and removes their sovereign immunity from US antitrust suits.

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas producers, refiners, and marketers, who would face new antitrust liability for supply decisions and greater scrutiny of mergers and information sharing. Foreign oil states would lose immunity from US lawsuits and could face enforcement actions.
analysis.who_pays_short: Oil and gas producers and foreign oil cartels

drawbacks.text: The NOPEC provision would invite retaliation against US oil companies and diplomatic friction with producer states; critics have long argued that suing foreign states over oil pricing would do little to lower prices at the pump and could provoke supply reprisals.

The prohibition on withholding supply turns on a company's primary intention, which courts would have to infer from costs and export prices; oil companies argued the standard is vague and could chill legitimate export and logistics decisions.

The bill was introduced amid high gas prices with limited time left in the session, and much of its content — studies, a task force, a report — would have produced information rather than immediate relief at the pump.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For consumers, the gains would have been real but gradual: new tools against deliberate supply withholding, better information on whether past merger settlements worked, and a path to suing foreign oil cartels. The strongest objection is the diplomatic and retaliation risk of the NOPEC provision, plus the difficulty of proving intent to withhold. On balance, the bill's burdens fall on oil companies and foreign producer states, not on ordinary households — and it never became law, so none of these effects occurred.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the House Judiciary Committee, which never acted on it; no hearing, markup, or floor vote happened before the Congress ended in January 2007.

narrative.text: Rep. John Conyers introduced the bill on May 3, 2006, with 10 cosponsors (9 Democrats and 1 Republican), including Judiciary members like Steve Chabot and Adam Schiff.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary the same day; that was the last action of record.
The committee took no further action — no markup, no report, no floor vote — and the bill died when the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil and gas companies, which avoided new antitrust liability and scrutiny of their supply and pricing decisions, and OPEC, which kept its immunity from US lawsuits. Consumers saw no change.

for.name: Rep. John Conyers Jr.
for.role: House Judiciary Committee ranking Democrat; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on May 3, 2006, as gas prices were high, and made its first floor appearance via introductory remarks in the Congressional Record.

for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction, giving it bipartisan sponsorship on the committee to which it was referred.

for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, making the original support 9 Democrats and 1 Republican.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee leadership
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over antitrust legislation
against.what_they_did: Held the bill after its May 3, 2006 referral — no hearing, markup, or vote was ever scheduled.

against.name: Oil and gas industry
against.what_they_did: Would have faced new supply-withholding liability and merger scrutiny under the bill; no industry advocacy appears in the record, but the bill targets its core pricing and supply practices.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was 9 Democrats and 1 Republican among 10 cosponsors, so the bill drew token GOP support but was framed by a Democratic sponsor; no votes were ever taken.

industries.industry: Oil and gas producers and refiners
industries.note: The bill would have made withholding or diverting fuel to raise prices unlawful and triggered a review of merger standards and past divestitures. Consumers would have gained price protection; the industry would have gained liability.

industries.industry: Foreign state oil producers (OPEC members and other petroleum exporters)
industries.note: NOPEC would have stripped them of sovereign immunity for collective production limits or price setting that affect US markets, exposing them to Justice Department antitrust suits. Their cartel pricing raises costs for US consumers.
